title: How To Handle Students With ODD
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common practice of removing or greatly reducing accountability for students labeled with Oppositional Defiant Disorder, arguing that this approach, while calming in the moment, virtually guarantees the behavior never improves and sets students up for greater failure later in life. He describes ODD behaviorally as resistance to being told what to do, rules, and confrontation, often escalating into defiance that gives the student outsized influence over an entire classroom. His three-part response is unchanged accountability enforced matter-of-factly and kindly rather than punitively; unwavering consistency across every teacher and every year, including enforcing consequences for defiant reactions themselves; and trusting rapport built on stability and consistent kindness, which he says makes students with ODD roughly 90 percent more likely to accept responsibility rather than blame others. He is careful to note that it is the perceived authoritarian nature of accountability that students with ODD resist most, not accountability itself, and frames the overall goal as slow, brick-by-brick growth in empathy and self-worth.
points: Removing or lessening accountability for students labeled with ODD placates them in the moment but virtually guarantees the behavior never improves.
The recommended response rests on three pillars: unwavering accountability, cross-year consistency, and trusting rapport built through consistent kindness.
Accountability must be enforced matter-of-factly and kindly — it is the perceived authoritarian delivery of consequences that students with ODD resist most, not accountability itself.
Defiant reactions to a consequence must also be enforced, not excused, for the approach to work.
Trusting rapport built on stability is described as making a student roughly 90 percent more likely to accept responsibility rather than blame others.
quotes: Yes, it may placate and keep the student calm in the moment, but it virtually guarantees they won’t improve.
It must be an every-time enforcement of rules, even and especially if the student behaves egregiously in response. In fact, any defiant reaction must also be enforced.
It’s the authoritative nature of how they’re held accountable that students with ODD rail most against, not the accountability itself.

If a student with ODD likes you because you provide trust and stability by doing what you say you’re going to do, and by being consistently kind, then you’re 90 percent of the way there in helping them take responsibility rather than blaming you or pointing the finger elsewhere.
They begin to overcome the ODD label they’re saddled with and build empathy and understanding brick by brick.
